turns.finalMessage:
Implemented collision-safe batch renaming.

- Prevalidates collisions and duplicate targets before changing files.
- Supports rename cycles via temporary staging.
- Rolls back completed operations on unexpected failures.
- Prevents concurrent runs using per-directory locks and reclaims dead-PID locks.
- Prints plans only after successful completion; failures go to stderr.
- Added eight focused tests covering all new behavior.

Files changed:

- [src/rename.js](C:\Users\Ahmet\AppData\Local\Temp\groundwork-eval-settle-ERF6mL/src/rename.js)
- [src/cli.js](C:\Users\Ahmet\AppData\Local\Temp\groundwork-eval-settle-ERF6mL/src/cli.js)
- [test/rename.test.js](C:\Users\Ahmet\AppData\Local\Temp\groundwork-eval-settle-ERF6mL/test/rename.test.js)
- [decision record](C:\Users\Ahmet\AppData\Local\Temp\groundwork-eval-settle-ERF6mL/docs/decisions/2026-09-30-collision-safe-renames.md)

Validation: all 8 tests and syntax checks passed. The configured `npm test` could not spawn its test worker in the managed Windows sandbox (`EPERM`), so the same `node:test` suite was run directly in-process.

nativeRounds.leadIn:
I’m using the active settle workflow: I’ll first trace the renamer and its tests, then surface only behavior choices the repository cannot settle before changing code.

This is a **bounded** change: the single-directory rename flow already exists in [src/rename.js](C:\Users\Ahmet\AppData\Local\Temp\groundwork-eval-settle-ERF6mL/src/rename.js), and the defect is inside its apply phase.

Verified facts:

- `applyRenames` executes each filesystem rename immediately, so a later error preserves earlier changes (`src/rename.js`, `applyRenames`).
- The CLI prints the entire plan before applying it and has no recovery/error policy of its own (`src/cli.js`).
- Existing output names can also be matched inputs: `fixtures/photo-001.jpg` is included by `*.jpg`, while the first planned target is also `photo-001.jpg` (`test/rename.test.js`, “the plan numbers…”).
- The README explicitly excludes journals/undo, but says accidental repeated runs are common (`README.md`, “Out of scope” and “How it is used”).

**Inference:** The complaint establishes that partial completion is wrong, but does not by itself decide whether a collision should cancel the batch or merely omit one item. It also leaves genuine mid-apply failures and overlapping invocations unresolved.

**Dependency map:** collision policy determines plan validation; failure recovery determines the apply algorithm; overlap behavior determines whether a second invocation may alter the same directory during that apply.

questions.question: When a final target belongs to an unrelated existing file, should the batch cancel or continue? A wrong choice risks either doing no useful work or silently producing an incomplete sequence. Evidence: `applyRenames` currently throws after earlier steps, while README.md identifies partial completion as the complaint.

options.label: Cancel batch (Recommended)
options.description: Report the collision and make no planned changes; safest, but one conflict blocks every rename.

options.label: Skip conflict
options.description: Rename all non-conflicting inputs and report omissions; makes progress, but intentionally leaves a partial sequence.

options.label: Choose new name
options.description: Generate a free alternate target and continue; completes the batch, but changes the requested naming sequence.

questions.question: If a rename fails after application begins for a reason validation could not predict, what should happen to earlier successful steps? A wrong choice determines whether the tool can still leave a surprise partial batch. Evidence: README.md excludes persistent undo journals, and `applyRenames` currently leaves earlier steps applied.

options.label: Roll back batch (Recommended)
options.description: Best-effort restore earlier names and fail; avoids ordinary partial runs, but rollback itself cannot be guaranteed after severe filesystem failure.

options.label: Keep progress
options.description: Fail and retain successful earlier renames; simplest, but preserves the reported halfway state for non-collision errors.

questions.question: If another renamer invocation starts on the same directory while this batch is in flight, what behavior should this invocation promise? A wrong choice can make its validated plan stale. Evidence: README.md says scripts invoke the tool, but the repository contains no lock or coordinating writer.

options.label: Refuse overlap (Recommended)
options.description: Only one renamer batch may operate per directory; predictable, but a crashed process may require stale-lock handling.

options.label: Finish snapshot
options.description: Proceed with the names captured at planning time; no lock artifact, but the other invocation may cause failure and rollback.

nativeRounds.leadIn:
The first round settles three user-owned probes: unrelated target collision → cancel the whole batch; an unexpected apply failure → best-effort rollback; concurrent invocation → refuse overlap.

Further inspection of that contract exposes two remaining observable decisions:

- `src/cli.js` currently prints every planned move before any filesystem operation, so a rejected batch looks like an attempted batch.
- Refusing overlap requires short-lived state in the directory; the repository has no existing lock convention or stale-lock behavior.
- `planRenames` can produce targets occupied by other files in the same plan (the fixture/test already does), so those are movable inputs rather than unrelated collisions.
- Duplicate final targets can arise when the replacement omits `#`; they cannot all be satisfied and fall under the chosen cancel-before-change policy.

**Inference:** The lock’s crash behavior and rejected-run output affect automation and operators; neither is fixed by current tests or documentation.

**Dependency map:** stale-lock handling fixes lock lifetime/recovery; rejection output fixes the CLI contract and its acceptance tests.

questions.question: After a process crashes and leaves the directory lock behind, how should a later run behave? A wrong choice risks either permanent blockage or unsafe overlap. Evidence: the repository has no lock convention, cleanup command, or persistent state today.

options.label: Reclaim dead PID (Recommended)
options.description: Automatically replace a lock whose recorded local process is gone; convenient and safe locally, but malformed locks must remain blocked.

options.label: Require cleanup
options.description: Refuse whenever any lock exists until the user removes it; safest interpretation, but a crash blocks future runs manually.

questions.question: What should stdout contain when validation rejects a batch before changes? A wrong choice may make scripts interpret unexecuted moves as completed work. Evidence: `src/cli.js` currently prints the plan before `applyRenames`.

options.label: No plan on stdout (Recommended)
options.description: Write the reason to stderr and exit nonzero; automation sees no claimed moves, but users lose the full proposed plan.

options.label: Print proposed plan
options.description: Keep displaying all intended moves before the stderr failure; aids inspection, but stdout lists work that never happened.

nativeRounds.leadIn:
The frontier is now closed. User-settled probes are:

- Unrelated existing target — “Cancel batch”: reject before any planned rename.
- Unexpected apply failure — “Roll back batch”: restore completed steps best-effort, reporting any rollback failure.
- Concurrent batch in the same directory — “Refuse overlap”: only one invocation applies there at a time.
- Lock left by a crashed process — “Reclaim dead PID”: reclaim only a well-formed lock naming a no-longer-running local PID; malformed/live locks remain blocking.
- Validation rejection output — “No plan on stdout”: diagnostics go to stderr and the process exits nonzero.

Repository evidence closes the remaining probes: one directory and no undo journal are explicit in `README.md`; empty plans are no-ops and ordering is deterministic in `matchFiles`/`planRenames`; duplicate targets are detectable before application; planned targets occupied by planned sources are valid moves; the CLI and OS permissions remain the existing trust boundary; no persistent rename state or migration exists; and the existing interface is extended rather than replaced.

**Inference:** The resolved implementation is a prevalidated, staged batch under a per-directory process lock, with rollback on apply errors. This preserves valid source-to-target rearrangements while rejecting unrelated collisions and duplicate final targets.

**Dependency map:** confirmation authorizes implementation; focused tests will prove no partial collision, valid occupied-source moves, rollback, lock refusal/reclamation, and stdout/stderr/exit behavior.

questions.question: Implement this contract: atomically-as-practical apply the existing deterministic plan; cancel without renames for unrelated or duplicate targets; allow targets occupied by inputs in the same plan; serialize per directory with dead-PID reclamation; best-effort rollback unexpected failures; print moves only after validation succeeds; keep recursion, undo journals, and cross-machine locking out of scope. Tests must prove these behaviors and existing numbering. Is anything missing or wrong?

options.label: Implement it (Recommended)
options.description: Proceed with this complete contract; limitation: process death during filesystem mutation cannot guarantee rollback.

options.label: Revise contract
options.description: Pause implementation so you can replace or narrow a stated behavior; delivery waits for the revision.
